stem.en: Meena scrapes her knee on the school playground. Two days later, the scrape is red and a little swollen, and there is some pus in it. Which part of her blood has collected at the scrape?

text.en: Red blood cells, because their iron-rich haemoglobin makes the scrape look red.

feedback.en: No. Haemoglobin makes blood red, but the redness and swelling of an infection come from white blood cells collecting there.

text.en: Platelets, because they gather wherever the skin is hurt and form a clot.

feedback.en: No. Platelets help a clot to form at a fresh cut. Redness, swelling and pus a few days later are signs of infection.

text.en: Plasma, because the liquid part of blood leaks out and slowly turns into pus.

feedback.en: No. Plasma is the liquid part of blood. Pus forms where white blood cells collect at an infected area.

text.en: White blood cells, which collect at infected areas.

feedback.en: Yes. White blood cells collect at an infected area, causing redness, swelling and sometimes pus.

explanation.en: Redness, swelling and pus are signs of an infection. White blood cells (WBCs) collect at infected areas, and this causes the redness and swelling, and sometimes pus. Platelets help clotting at a fresh cut, and haemoglobin in red blood cells gives blood its red colour.

hints.en: Is this a fresh cut, or an infection a few days later?
Which blood cells gather where there are germs?
